findings.quote: It builds up where the chain drags on the bottom and close to the swivel.
findings.note: Domain knowledge of aids-to-navigation mooring maintenance leans to B: abrasion concentrates in the ground section that works on the seabed and at connecting hardware such as the swivel. Distractors are substantive, though — C states a real competing failure mode (corrosion vs abrasion), A a figure only a text could supply, D a plausible siting effect — so the exact key is not decided blind. Options are parallel in length and assertion strength; no form-only tell.

findings.quote: It may be riding the edge of the circle its chain allows, not dragging its sinker.
findings.note: Knowledge of buoy moorings supplies the watch-circle explanation, so C is the domain-favoured pick, and the same knowledge marks B's relation as inverted (more scope, not less, widens the circle). Both eliminations are domain reasoning, not form: the previous run's hedge-asymmetry basis no longer holds now that B is hedged ('is likely to') alongside C's 'may be', with A additionally softened by 'about' — two hedged, no lone-hedge tell. Distractors are substantive (A is a real 3:1 scope rule, D a plausible operational response), so this is world knowledge, not a structural leak.

findings.quote: What keeping a floating light on station involves, and an unsettled argument about slack.
findings.note: Two options fall passage-blind on scope alone: A is framed as a narrow historical episode ('in the years before buoys marked the shoal') and D introduces a cost thesis no other option touches. That leaves B against C, and the choice between a balanced survey with an unsettled dispute and an advocacy piece for loggers genuinely needs the passage. B is a breadth-heuristic lean, not a decided answer; the distractor set is the canonical too-narrow / wrong-thesis / off-angle trio, which is normal main-idea design rather than a leak.

findings.quote: To suggest that the old keepers may have watched their position more closely than today's crews.
findings.note: ARGUABLE: the case is assembled from two true citations rather than refuted outright. The lightship's logs "carry, watch after watch, three bearings taken on the shore marks" and Fewtrell "remembers the mate chalking a corrected position by the companionway", while of the modern tenders the text says Prigent's "recordings put a figure on something the crews had only estimated" - a reader can take that juxtaposition as a contrast in rigour, and the option is hedged ("may have"). Beatable: the passage states its own reason in a causal clause - the bearings were taken "because a moored ship does not sit still either and her keepers knew it" - so they are evidence for positional uncertainty (the key), the word "either" links the lightship to the buoys rather than contrasting them, the paragraph closes on "Where we were over it was another question", and "only estimated" concerns crews estimating buoy wander (a missing instrument, not inattention). The prompt asks why the writer mentions the lightship, and the text supplies that reason itself.

findings.quote: as much as 35 metres from their charted places
findings.note: class 4: numeral style breaks the passage's own established convention — every other measurement and count is spelled out ("thirty-one metres of it for eleven metres of water", "two hundred and fourteen floating aids", "eleven fresh links", "forty minutes"), so a copy editor would normalise this one figure; editor's rewrite: 'as much as thirty-five metres from their charted places'.

findings.quote: It is heaviest on the aids moored inshore, where the channel water is narrow.
findings.note: class 3: "the channel water is narrow" is not an English collocation — the passage's own "where the water is narrow" works because "narrow water(s)" is fixed trade idiom, but premodifying it with "channel" makes a compound noun of which "narrow" cannot naturally be predicated; editor's rewrite: 'where the channel is narrow'.

findings.quote: the buoys laid longest sit as much as 35 metres from their charted places for hours together
findings.note: class 4 (register/house style): the piece spells out every other quantity in words - 'thirty-one metres of it for eleven metres of water', 'two hundred and fourteen floating aids', 'forty minutes', 'thirty-one years', 'eleven fresh links' - so this lone numeral for a measurement breaks the style the text has set for itself, and a copy editor would harmonise it. Editor's rewrite: 'sit as much as thirty-five metres from their charted places'.

findings.quote: a lift, a scrape, a fresh lamp and a relay take about forty minutes
findings.note: class 3: 'a relay' garden-paths the reader into the electrical/handover sense; the meaning is 'laying the buoy again', which British house style hyphenates precisely to avoid this collision. Editor's rewrite: 'a lift, a scrape, a fresh lamp and a re-lay take about forty minutes'.

findings.quote: It is heaviest on the aids moored inshore, where the channel water is narrow.
findings.note: class 3: noun-stacked 'channel water' is an awkward pairing - a channel is narrow, water is shallow; the passage's own 'where the water is narrow' works because 'narrow water' is settled nautical idiom, but prefixing 'channel' breaks it. Editor's rewrite: 'where the channel is narrow'.

findings.quote: the buoys laid longest sit as much as 35 metres from their charted places
findings.note: class 4: sole numeral among roughly twenty spelled-out quantities ('thirty-one metres', 'eleven metres', 'two hundred and fourteen', 'forty minutes', 'eleven fresh links'), so the piece's number style is internally inconsistent at one point. Defensible as an instrument-reading contrast, but a copy desk would query. Editor's rewrite: 'as much as thirty-five metres'.

findings.quote: Tuning can cost more than the bronze on a small bell, and less than it on a heavy one.
findings.note: Labour-vs-metal economics (metal cost scales with mass, lathe labour far less so) makes D the true real-world statement, and it is also the only two-sided conditional among three flat generalisations ('always takes a larger share', 'a single price for each kilo', 'far longer to tune'). The distractors are substantive trade claims a passage would have to decide, so this is world-knowledge answerability, not a form-only leak.

findings.quote: The bell has to leave the mould heavier, since the metal tuning removes must be there first.
findings.note: Standard founding practice - bells are cast with a tuning allowance because lathe tuning only removes metal - decides A on domain knowledge, and A's own justifying clause is close to self-evident. B, C and D are substantive claims a passage would still have to ground, so flag rather than a structural leak.

findings.quote: He treats the disagreement as a matter of taste that measurement can never settle.
findings.note: Two options fall passage-blind: B is undercut because A and C both presuppose an actual trial exists, and D's 'workshop folklore that the measurements have already disposed of' is the overreaching dismissal typical of filler. A (mild lean) versus C (even-handed) stays undecided without the text; lean C on expository-genre convention.

findings.quote: How a bell's partials are tuned, what that work costs, and how far founders take it.
findings.note: Main-idea item in which D is the compound scope statement that largely subsumes A's cost angle, while B ('recover less of the bronze ... than they generally suppose') is too narrow to be a thesis and C lists a different text's subject. Breadth-wins is a form-level tell, but A remains a live competitor if the text really is price-focused, so partial rather than decided.

findings.quote: and less than it on a heavy one
findings.note: class 3: grammatical comparative ellipsis, but the pronoun 'it' sits next to 'a small bell' and only resolves to 'the bronze' on a second pass — a copy editor would bracket it and query the referent, and in option text (which must be unambiguous at speed for a Swedish examinee) would spell it out. Editor's rewrite: 'and less than the bronze on a heavy one'. No other conviction: the passage is native-quality British magazine prose — no article errors, no false friends, no Swedish interference, consistent British orthography ('mould', 'neighbours', 'tonne'), consistent no-Oxford-comma house style, and genuinely native idiom ('came ninth', 'the better part of a day', 'forty-odd', 'keeps its bins swept'). Register holds one serious-magazine voice throughout with no AI boilerplate, and texture is concrete (named founders, dated 2019 Ockthorne trial, reconciling weights 240/12/228, hedged claims, dry wit).

findings.quote: The animals were up at the warm end while the afternoon heat lasted, and out at the cool end after dark.
findings.note: Passage-blind I can discount C (a gradient staying as wide at dawn as in the late afternoon is thermally implausible for a void that cools overnight) and lean away from A (day-roosting bats normally hold the warm end while the sun is on the roof), which concentrates the mass on B and D; D is my lean. B - heat rising from the rooms below - stays a substantive and generally true alternative, so the passage is still needed to decide. This is domain reasoning, not a form tell.

findings.quote: Cast boxes work as well as timber ones provided they are hung high on a sunny wall.
findings.note: C is eliminable on scope alone - the stem asks what is suggested about two specific occupied boxes while C answers about cast boxes in general - and D is counter-directional (aggregate that 'gave up its heat more quickly' would argue against occupancy, not for it), leaving A against B. A is my lean, but B (the only cast boxes on a south-facing wall) is an equally substantive competing explanation of the same anomaly, so the item is not decided blind.

findings.quote: Convinced: the writer agrees with her that what a box is made of hardly matters at all.
findings.note: The two extreme stances are discountable blind - A because the sheet's own interest in cast versus timber boxes makes wholesale agreement that material 'hardly matters at all' unlikely, D less firmly - leaving the two qualified stances B and C at roughly even odds. Oyelaran's objection is never stated in the stems, so nothing decides between them: better than chance, not answerable.

findings.quote: Why some purpose-built replacement roosts are taken up by bats while others stand empty.
findings.note: Standard main-idea item: C overstates ('give up counting animals altogether'), while A and D name real but subordinate threads (planning conditions, a disagreement), and the sibling stems - boxes on a converted school, roof voids, occupied cast boxes, temperature - make B the topical fit. The blind answerability comes from the sibling stems and ordinary main-idea option shapes rather than from any tell inside this item, so flag rather than kill.

findings.quote: most of the boxes that failed had been opened in June or July
findings.note: class 3 (idiom/collocation): a bat box is fitted, hung or put up, not 'opened' - the verb belongs to buildings and services, not to a wall-mounted box. The passage itself uses the right verb two sentences later ('those fitted between September and February') and elsewhere ('all fitted out of season', 'You can hang the finest box in the county'), so the slip is visible on the page. editor's rewrite: 'most of the boxes that failed had been fitted in June or July'.

findings.quote: the space near the ridge can stand close to thirty degrees
findings.note: class 2 (preposition choice): a reading stands AT a figure; with the preposition dropped the space appears to 'stand' a temperature rather than register one. editor's rewrite: 'the space near the ridge can stand at close to thirty degrees'.

findings.quote: most of the boxes that failed had been opened in June or July
findings.note: class 3 idiom/collocation: a bat box is put up, fitted, hung or erected - it is never 'opened'. The piece uses the right verbs everywhere else ('they went up', 'those fitted between September and February', 'You can hang the finest box in the county'), so the odd verb reads as a slip rather than variation. Editor's rewrite: 'most of the boxes that failed had been put up in June or July'

findings.quote: most of the boxes that failed had been opened in June or July
findings.note: class 3: collocation miss - a bat box is fitted, hung or put up, not 'opened' (buildings and exhibitions open; boxes do not). The passage itself uses the right verbs everywhere else ('those fitted between September and February', 'twenty-four boxes went up on nine buildings', 'You can hang the finest box in the county'), so the outlier reads as a slip rather than a choice. Editor's rewrite: 'most of the boxes that failed had been put up in June or July'.

findings.quote: the space near the ridge can stand close to thirty degrees
findings.note: class 3: 'stand' before a figure normally takes 'at' ('the temperature stood at thirty degrees'), and with 'the space' as subject against the parallel clause's 'sits ten or twelve degrees below it' the bare 'stand close to' reads clipped. Editor's rewrite: 'the space near the ridge can sit at close to thirty degrees'.

findings.quote: Luft tränger in, veden brinner upp i stället för att förkolna, och kolningen går förlorad.
findings.note: WORLD_KNOWLEDGE shading into general recall, blind pick B: air ingress turning pyrolysis into combustion is the defining fact about a charcoal kiln and is decidable with no text at all. D is an absolute foil ('ofelbart ... oavsett'). A and C stay plausible enough that the key is not left alone in the plausible set, so flag rather than a RECALL_ONLY kill - but this is the weakest passage-dependence in the unit.

findings.quote: Kolet smulades sönder vid omlastning och måste fram kort väg, medan tjäran tålde långa transporter.
findings.note: WORLD_KNOWLEDGE, blind pick D: charcoal friability versus barrelled tar is the textbook reason and needs no passage. Aggravating factor for adjudication: the stem sheet itself supplies the fact, since q:1 option C states 'Kolet blir ofta sprött och smulas sönder redan vid den första omlastningen på brukets slädar', so a solver working the sheet in order can corroborate D without reading the text.

findings.quote: Tjäran låg still i sina tunnor
findings.note: class 5/6: bare predicative 'still' is the spoken/colloquial variant (as in 'ligg still!'); edited sakprosa uses the invariable standard form 'stilla', and the repo's 2.7 MB authentic-HP corpus shows only 'stilla' in this use (every bare 'still' hit there is English ELF text). In an otherwise high-register essay ('tålde världen olika väl', 'i skarpa ordalag') it reads as a register/form slip. Native alternative: 'Tjäran låg stilla i sina tunnor'.

findings.quote: Låntagaren fick säd och lämnade tillbaka lika mycket vid skörden, jämte ett tillägg på vanligen en åttondel.
findings.note: WORLD_KNOWLEDGE (blind pick C). Domain knowledge of Swedish sockenmagasin decides it: grain was lent in spring and repaid in kind after harvest with interest in natura, commonly one eighth. No form-only asymmetry - A (repayment in money), B (surcharge set annually by the sockenstämma) and D (collective lending at crop failure) are parallel in length and register and are all substantively possible arrangements a passage would have to settle.

findings.quote: Kyrkvärden förvarade båda nycklarna och kunde därför öppna magasinet utan att någon annan var närvarande.
findings.note: WORLD_KNOWLEDGE (blind pick A). Knowledge of magasinsordningar - two locks with keys held by different men, entry in the ledger at the moment of lending, shared accountability for the accounts - makes B, C and D read as control failures no ordinance would prescribe, leaving A. A near-structural pattern supports it (three options close on a slackened-control clause: 'utan att någon annan var närvarande', 'behövde inte ... förrän', 'svarade ensam', while A states a sanction), but seeing that pattern as decisive requires assuming the ordinance's purpose was tight control, which is domain inference rather than pure form - hence major, not lethal.

findings.quote: Att han överdriver sparbankernas roll så till den grad att ingen enda av socknarna i boken stöder sambandet.
findings.note: PARTIALLY (blind pick D). No world knowledge is available - Grimlund and the district are invented - so the lean is formal: C is the only option carrying an absolute ('ingen enda') and is a same-topic overstated twin of D, and in such a pair the measured member is the conventional key; D is also the only option whose subject is the explanation itself ('Att den vilar på sparbankerna') rather than the author ('Att han ...'), matching the stem's focus on 'Grimlunds förklaring'. A (the 1863 kommunreform omission) and B (a single stämmoprotokoll carrying the argument) stay substantively open, so the item is materially better than chance blind but not decided.

findings.quote: Att han förbigår kommunreformen 1863, trots att den gjorde det oklart vem som ägde magasinen.
findings.note: ARGUABLE: the substance of this criticism is genuinely in the passage — the reviewer does fault Grimlund for underplaying the alternative explanations ('Men detta står i förbigående, på en dryg sida, och läsaren får själv väga ihop det', 'det hade varit klädsamt att säga det rakt ut') — and the option's second clause is verbatim supported ('kommunreformen 1863 lämnade oklart vem som egentligen ägde magasinet, socknen eller den nya kommunen'). The lure is lexical: 'förbigår' sits one clitic away from 'i förbigående', a phrase the passage uses twice for Grimlund treating something lightly. The case is beatable and no complaint would survive: 'förbigår' asserts omission, and the passage says he raises it himself — 'Han antyder själv två. ... Och kommunreformen 1863 lämnade oklart ...'. The prompt delimiter 'mot Grimlunds förklaring till att magasinen försvann' also points at the explanation he actually advances, which is what the key restates ('bokens eget bilagematerial talar delvis emot honom ... de tidigaste nedläggningarna i Hässle härad flera decennier före den första sparbanken i samma härad'). Flagged, not killed — the key remains clearly best.

findings.quote: jämte ett tillägg — vanligen en åttondel — också det i råg
findings.note: class 2 (English punctuation habit): the text uses the English em dash U+2014 as tankstreck throughout (5 occurrences incl. the byline) and no en dash at all; Swedish edited sakprosa sets tankstreck as a spaced en dash. The repo's own authentic HP corpus shows 5139 en dashes against 6 em dashes. Native alternative: 'jämte ett tillägg – vanligen en åttondel – också det i råg'.

findings.quote: de partier som inte tjänar något argument alls
findings.note: class 6 (idiomatic temperature): Swedish 'tjäna' collocates with syfte/sak/tes, so 'tjänar något argument' reads as the English 'serve an argument' stretched onto the Swedish frame. Native alternative: 'de partier som inte tjänar något syfte alls'.

findings.quote: de partier som inte tjänar något argument alls
findings.note: class 6: idiomatic temperature. Swedish 'tjäna' takes abstract objects productively ('tjäna ett syfte', 'tjäna en sak'), but 'tjäna ett argument' is a thin collocation that maps one-to-one onto English 'serve an argument'; a copy editor may pause on it. Native alternative: 'de partier som inte tjänar något syfte alls' or 'de partier som inte driver någon tes'.

findings.quote: De hade ett givet mått i fyrkant, medan tjockleken blev den som vinterns kyla råkade ge.
findings.note: WORLD_KNOWLEDGE, blind pick C: lake-ice thickness is set by the winter, so harvested blocks are cut to a standard plan measure with the thickness left to the season. A is the physical inverse of that and B is close to self-refuting ('vägde alltid omkring hundrafemtio kilo, oavsett hur kall vintern hade varit'). D remains a substantive detail a passage could carry, so flag.
